title: The carob tree (Taanit 23a)
hookLine: an old man plants a tree he'll never eat from, for his grandchildren

cards: Somebody planted the big tree on your street. Somebody dug the well, laid the stones of the oldest building in town, started the library, wrote down the recipe your family still makes. Most of them never knew your name.
They did the work and left it for whoever came next. The Talmud tells of Honi, the circle-drawer, walking down a road and meeting one of those people: a man, planting a tree.

teach.h: HOW LONG UNTIL IT BEARS FRUIT?
teach.b: It's the same page of tractate Taanit as yesterday's circle. You met this scene once before, with Rabbi Tarfon, as a picture of work you won't finish. Today, look closer.
Honi sees a man planting a carob tree. Retellings usually make him old; the Talmud just says a certain man. Honi asks: how long until this tree gives fruit?
Seventy years, the man says. Honi presses: are you sure you'll live another seventy years? Listen to the order of the answer.
He doesn't start with the future.
He starts with what he found. I found the world with carob trees in it. Just as my ancestors planted for me, I'm planting for my children.
Then he passes it on. The planting grows out of the noticing. In the Psalms, seventy years is a full life, so he's planting past the edge of his own, on purpose.
The story keeps going, and Honi's next seventy years will surprise him. More on that soon. For today, stay with the word found.
It's a small picture of how a tradition works at all.
Every teaching on this path, somebody planted. They memorized it, copied it, argued over it, carried it through exile, and passed it down to people they'd never meet. Including you.

how: The carob story is often told on Tu BiShvat, the new year of trees, when some Jews plant trees or eat fruits such as carob.

games.q: you're planting a tree that won't fruit for seventy years. a stranger asks: will you live to eat from it? what do you say first?
o: I found carob trees here, so I plant for my children.
games.why: he started with what he'd found: I found the world with carob trees. as my ancestors planted for me, I plant for my children.

practice: Look around and name three things in reach that someone made or planted before you arrived, a chair, a road, a word you use, and silently thank people you'll never meet.
Then think of one small thing you could start that someone will enjoy after you: a seed in a pot, a note in a book, a family recipe taught to a kid.

wordCard.voice: Carob, the slow tree a man plants though it won't bear fruit for seventy years, because his ancestors planted for him.

orig.note: Hebrew: carob, the slow tree in the story.
